passage: Note, student counselling, Thursday. Karthik, 20, asked for advice before Diwali. He does not believe in God but does not want to hurt his family, and his mother expects him at the puja. I asked what he wants. He said, "I want to be there, and I don't want to pretend." I did not tell him what to believe. We practised what he could say. On Monday he came back. He had told his mother in the kitchen, "Amma, I don't pray the way you do, but I'd love to sit with you and light the lamps." She was quiet, then handed him the matchbox. He said he felt nervous first, then warm. I asked whether he had been honest and still belonged. He said yes. I will check in after the holidays. Deepika, counsellor

qa.q: What did Karthik's mother do after he spoke in the kitchen?
qa.a: She was quiet, then handed him the matchbox.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel telling his mother, according to the note?
qa.a: Karthik felt nervous at first and then warm, since he could be honest and still belong.

qa.q: Which choice by Karthik kept honesty and belonging together?
qa.a: Karthik told his mother gently that he does not pray the way she does but would love to sit with her and light the lamps, without pretending faith.

qa.q: How might Karthik's mother have felt handing him the matchbox?
qa.a: Probably touched and accepting. After being quiet, she gave him a real part in the puja.

grounding: A non-believer joins a family puja for love and tradition without pretending faith, being gently open about it.

passage: Tuesday night. Went to Ajji's Ganesh puja today. I have never believed, and I told Ajji last year I'm not sure about God. She just said, "Come anyway, beta." So I did, in a red kurta with the flower basket. I didn't say the mantras, but I stood beside her while she sang the aarti, and the smell of camphor and marigold took me back to being five. I held her hand. Tenzin, my friend from the hostel, texted, "Weird to go if you don't believe?" I wrote back, "It's not about proving anything. It's about her and me." Ajji whispered afterwards, "You don't have to believe, you just have to be here." I cried a little on the bus. Not sad. Just full. Irawati

qa.q: What did Ajji say when Irawati told her about doubting God last year?
How does Irawati feel at the end of the day?
qa.a: Irawati feels full and moved, not sad. The camphor and marigold smell and holding Ajji's hand bring back childhood warmth.

qa.q: Which choice by Irawati let honesty and belonging sit together?
qa.a: Irawati went to the puja, stood beside Ajji and held her hand without saying the mantras, and was honest that it is about Ajji and Irawati, not about proving anything.

qa.q: How might Ajji have felt having Irawati beside her?
qa.a: Probably happy and reassured. She had invited Irawati anyway and whispered that just being there is enough.

grounding: A non-believer joins a family puja for love and tradition without pretending faith, and stays open about it.
